title: Tree Traversal
summary: Visit every node in a small binary tree using left, root, right order. Trace the calls and compare the same tree in six languages.
introduction: Think of visiting every room in a small tree house. You need a plan so no room is missed. A tree traversal is a plan for visiting each node in a tree. Here we use inorder: visit the left branch, record the current node, then visit the right branch.
learningObjectives: Follow left, root, right order in a binary tree
Explain when inorder traversal prints sorted values

blocks.text: A node is one item in a tree. The root is the top node. A binary tree allows each node at most two children, called left and right. An empty child is written as null, nullptr, NULL, or None in these languages.
Our tree has root 4. Its left child is 2 and its right child is 6. Node 2 has children 1 and 3. Nodes 1, 3, and 6 have no children. Every tab builds these same links.
Inorder means left, current node, right. The function uses recursion: it follows the same plan for a smaller branch. An empty child is the base case, where it returns immediately.

items: Start at 4, but do not record it yet. Go left to 2, then left again to 1.
Node 1 has no left child, so record 1. Its right child is also empty. Return to 2.
Record 2, then visit its right child and record 3. The whole left branch is done.
Return to the root and record 4. Finally visit its right child and record 6. The order is 1, 2, 3, 4, 6.

blocks.text: The same program in six languages

Choose the language you are learning. Each tab solves the same problem and prints the same result. JavaScript can run in this page. The other tabs need separate local tools: a C11 compiler, a C++17 compiler, Python 3, .NET 8 or later for C#, or Java 17. Use Program.cs for C# and Main.java for Java.

variants.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, left=None, right=None):
        self.value = value
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def inorder(node, order):
    if node is None:
        return
    inorder(node.left, order)
    order.append(node.value)
    inorder(node.right, order)

root = Node(4, Node(2, Node(1), Node(3)), Node(6))
order = []
inorder(root, order)
print(*order)

blocks.text: The list records each node once in left, root, right order. It is sorted because this example is also a binary search tree: smaller values lie to the left and larger values to the right. An arbitrary binary tree does not promise sorted inorder output.

An empty tree produces an empty visit list. One node is recorded once. The input must be a proper tree with no link back to an ancestor. A cyclic graph needs a visited check, as the graph traversal lessons show.

The C output array has five spaces for this five-node example. Increase its capacity if you add nodes. Other versions grow a list as needed. Repeated values in separate nodes are still visited separately.
Two other plans are preorder (current, left, right) and postorder (left, right, current). Moving the record step changes the plan. Keep the child calls in the chosen order.
How much work and extra room?
Let n be the number of nodes. Each node is visited once and has at most two child links to check, so traversal takes O(n) time.

Let h be the longest root-to-leaf path measured in nodes. Waiting calls need O(h) stack space. A balanced tree has h around log n; a long one-branch tree has h = n. This example also saves n output values, so total extra space is O(n). Printing each value during the visit would avoid that saved output list.

blocks.title: Try one small change
blocks.text: Change the right child value from 6 to 5 in your chosen tab. The structure stays the same, and the output should become 1 2 3 4 5. Follow the links to explain why only the last value changes.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Check for an empty node before reading its children. Also do not assume every binary tree is a binary search tree: inorder is sorted only when the tree obeys the search-tree ordering rule.
